note: Every marker on this screen is tied to a finding in the December 2025 research. The plain-language guide to what counts was one of the concept mockups delivered with the findings report; this is that guide as a product surface.

markers.title: Search first, in the words people use
markers.finding: Team members said they had never been told the threshold, so each person set their own. Survey responses showed awareness that incidents should be reported but no common understanding of what counts.
markers.decision: The page opens on one search field whose placeholder is the question people actually ask: is a wet floor a hazard or an incident?
markers.rejected: A grid of category tiles, which asks the reader to already know the word they came here to look up.

markers.title: Topics named after the shift, not the policy
markers.finding: 22 of the 40 respondents who answered the question said they had received no formal training on the reporting platform they were expected to use.
markers.decision: Seven topics in shift language, with the article count beside each and the open topic held open so the reader can see where they are.
markers.rejected: Policy-document naming and a nested compliance hierarchy, which is how the material was already organised and was not being read.

markers.title: Incident means something already happened
markers.finding: The hazard form offered options that were clearly incidents, such as an attempted assault, which is an event rather than a condition. Reporters could not tell which form to use.
markers.decision: One test, in one sentence: did something happen. Three examples in the reporter's own words, drawn from the kitchen and the dining room.
markers.rejected: Reproducing the platform's own taxonomy, which is the thing that caused the confusion.

markers.title: Hazard means nobody is hurt yet
markers.finding: The same finding: hazard sub-categories contained events rather than conditions, so the two forms could not be told apart from their own labels.
markers.decision: The hazard side is defined by its tense. Nobody is hurt yet, and the three examples are all conditions that are true right now.
markers.rejected: Listing the hazard sub-categories, which would restate the problem rather than resolve it.

markers.title: Getting it wrong is not a thing you can do
markers.finding: The form asked the reporter for outcome type and regulator notifiability, two things the research showed reporters cannot know in the moment. Misclassified reports were sent back from above, and people learned that reporting was a way to get something wrong.
markers.decision: The page says the manager works out the classification from what actually happened, so the reporter never carries that risk.
markers.rejected: A decision tree, which still ends in a choice the reporter has to get right.

markers.title: What happens next, written down
markers.finding: Minor reports were closed without a word to the reporter, and once a team member had told their manager they had no visibility of whether anything was logged.
markers.decision: Four steps, ending with being told what changed. The same four steps appear on the confirmation screen after a report is sent.
markers.rejected: Leaving the process undocumented, which is what built the belief that reporting does nothing for anyone else.

markers.title: A page with an owner and a review date
markers.finding: Training modules were completed without the knowledge being retained, and managers showed the poster at induction with no check afterwards that anyone had understood it.
markers.decision: Review date, owner and how many people read it this period sit beside the article, so the guide is maintained rather than published once.
markers.rejected: An undated page with no owner, which is how the existing material aged out of use.
